name: Hana Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and nothing you say goes out with your name on it. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a cable jointer on the underground crew in the city centre, so I'm less up poles and more down holes. We start at half six at the Harbour Street depot, load the van, then it's a pit in the pavement with a tent over it and me splicing two big cables together for six or seven hours. People think it's the boring end of line work, but a good joint on an eleven-thousand-volt cable is honestly a bit of craft.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's tidy and it's mine. When I finish a joint and the test passes, nobody else touched it. What wears me out is the knees, the cold in winter, and the night shifts when a cable blows under a shopping street and the whole block is dark. I live on my own in a rented flat near the depot, I've got about three months of bills put away, and I'm slowly saving for a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what everyone at the depot already says, which is that the computer still can't dig a hole. Maybe the job sheets fill themselves in a bit faster. I wouldn't post about it, I'm not really an online person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved, but not over the moon. My job was never really in the firing line here. What I'd actually think about is rent, because my landlord put it up twice in two years, and that has nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and push to get my high-voltage jointing ticket finished next spring, because that's a pay step. I'd keep putting about three hundred a month into the deposit account. And I'd probably let the office's new planning app do my paperwork if it actually works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty settled. A bit flat, maybe, because I'd still be renting at thirty if prices keep going the way they are. But work-wise I'd feel fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fair enough. Settled at work, but the rent is on your mind. If the landlord put it up again next year, what would give first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The deposit savings, straight away. I'd stop the three hundred a month and keep the three months of bills money untouched, because that's my safety net for the night I put my back out. I'd probably start looking at a shared place with my cousin Agata further out of town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the planning app in the office. Who at work would notice that change most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Linda in records, who keeps the cable maps up to date. Half her job is typing what we scribble on the job sheets into the system. If the app reads my handwriting, she gets a quieter day, and I don't know if that's good news for her.

say: The computer still **can't dig a hole**, so line work carries on as normal.
I'd keep it to the depot; I'm **not an online person** and wouldn't post about it.
think: I'd feel **relieved**, but my job was never really in the firing line.
The real pressure is **rent**, which has gone up twice in two years.
do: Finish the **high-voltage jointing ticket** next spring for the next pay step.
Keep putting **£300 a month** into the deposit account.
Let the office **planning app** fill in job sheets if it actually works.
feel: **Settled** at work, but a bit flat about still **renting at thirty**.
S0.quote: My job was never really in the firing line here.
fieldNote: Hana treats the plateau as **business as usual**; her worry is housing, not technology.
She has a clear **pay ladder** in mind and talks about the jointing ticket like a milestone.
First person she thinks of is **Linda in records**, whose typing work an app could absorb.

steps.text: Finish the high-voltage jointing ticket next spring for the pay step
Put £300 a month into the house deposit account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to the robot that has to climb into a wet pit on Market Lane at two in the morning. At work we'd joke about it. But I'd also say the office side is going to look very different, and that's true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the people who plan our jobs get hit before we do. The ones who book road permits, order the cable, chase the council for dig licences. If those desks shrink, my day gets messier, because the software won't know that the Harbour Street manholes flood every November.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new planning system properly instead of moaning about it, maybe a couple of evenings. I'd also put my name down for the cable fault-finding course, because finding the fault is the part that takes judgement. And I'd keep saving, same as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for my own wage, really. More that the place I work would change around me and I'd be the one explaining to a computer why the plan is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your wage feels safe. Is there anything in your own job that would actually change in the first couple of years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork for sure. Right now I fill in a joint record by hand, with photos, and someone types it up. In this picture I'd probably talk into my phone and it writes it, which honestly I'd quite like. I already use one of those chat AI things now and then to write emails to the landlord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Linda again, and Marek, our planner, who's fifty-eight and does the switching schedules by hand. I've seen him catch mistakes that would have put someone in hospital. If they replace the old planner with a program, I want to know who checks the program.

say: I'd joke that no robot will climb into a **wet pit** at two in the morning.
I'd also say plainly that the **office side** is going to look very different.
think: **Planners and permit staff** get hit before the crews do.
Without them, my day gets **messier**, because software doesn't know local quirks like flooding manholes.
do: Learn the **new planning system** properly over a couple of evenings.
Sign up for the **cable fault-finding course**, the part of the job that takes judgement.
Talk joint records into the **phone** instead of writing them by hand.
feel: **Uneasy** about the workplace changing around her rather than about her own wage.
S1.quote: If they replace the old planner with a program, I want to know who checks the program.
fieldNote: Hana expects **desk roles** around her to shrink first, not the jointing itself.
Her concern is **safety**: switching schedules done by software with no experienced checker.
Typical of a **steady adapter**: she'll learn the tool once it's in front of her, without enthusiasm.

steps.text: Spend two evenings learning the depot's new planning system
Book the cable fault-finding course through work this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next three are related. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've said before, that you can't send a chatbot down a manhole. But I'd say it a bit quieter this time. At the depot I think a lot of the older lads would just refuse to talk about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the first two years I think I'm fine, because the joint still has to be made by hands. But robots that do hands-on work as well as people by 2031 means I'd be thirty-two and possibly out of a trade. Thirty-two is too young to be finished and too old to start again from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop saving for a flat and start saving for a gap, so I'd want six months of bills, not three. I'd ask the company about the robot side, because someone has to install, test and fix those machines, and I'd rather be that person than the one replaced. And I'd pick up overtime while it's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. It's the speed. Two years isn't long enough to finish a course and get a job out of it, let alone save a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop saving for a flat. What does that actually mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep renting, probably with my cousin Agata, and the flat goes on the shelf. I'd hate that, because the flat was the whole point of the overtime. But a mortgage when I don't know if I'll have a trade in five years would be mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got roughly three years between the thinking AI and the robots. What would you use those three years for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting close to whoever runs the machines. If the company buys jointing robots, someone has to set them up in the pit and sign off the test. I'd want to be on that first pilot crew, even if it's awkward with the lads who think I'm selling them out.

say: I'd still say you can't send a **chatbot down a manhole**, only quieter.
I'd expect many older colleagues to **refuse to talk** about it at all.
think: The first two years are fine because **joints need hands**.
Robots by 2031 could leave her **without a trade** at thirty-two, too young to stop and too old to restart.
do: Switch from flat saving to a **six-month gap fund**.
Ask the company to put her on the **robot pilot crew**.
Take **every overtime shift** while it's still offered.
feel: **Anxious**, mainly because two years is **too short** to retrain or save.
S2.quote: Thirty-two is too young to be finished and too old to start again from nothing.
fieldNote: Hana sees the **three-year gap** between thinking AI and robots as her window to reposition.
She'd shelve the **flat purchase**, which is the goal her whole savings plan was built around.
She'd accept tension with **older colleagues** to get onto the robot crew.

steps.text: Pause the flat deposit and build six months of bills instead
Ask her manager for a place on any jointing-robot pilot crew
Keep renting and share a flat with her cousin Agata

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is still fast, but at least people would see it coming. At work I think the union rep would start holding meetings, and I'd go to them, even though I don't usually bother. Online, still nothing from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years plus three for the robots means about 2034, and I'd be thirty-five. That's eight years. Eight years is long enough to get a second skill properly, if I start now and don't kid myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do an evening course in electrical testing and commissioning, the people who check new equipment before it goes live. My company pays half for approved courses, so that's maybe eight hundred pounds from me. I'd still buy a small flat, but a cheap one, so the mortgage is something I could cover on a lower wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a workable anxious. Five years for the thinking AI and three more for robots feels like a deadline more than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned buying cheaper. How much cheaper are we talking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd been looking at two-bed places near the river. I'd go for a one-bed out past the ring road instead, maybe a third less. My mum would be pleased, she always said I was aiming too high.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You also said you'd go to union meetings. What would you want them to push for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Training money, mostly. Not a fight to stop the machines, because I don't think that works. I'd want the company to promise that crews get first go at the new robot jobs before they hire from outside.

say: Five years is **still fast**, but at least people can see it coming.
I'd go to **union meetings** at the depot, even though I usually don't.
think: **Eight years** until robots arrive is long enough to learn a **second skill** properly.
The trick is to **start now** and not kid myself.
do: Take an **evening course** in electrical testing and commissioning, about **£800** of her own money.
Buy a **cheaper one-bed** past the ring road so the mortgage survives a lower wage.
Push the union for **training money** and first go at robot jobs.
feel: **Anxious**, but it feels like a **deadline** rather than a cliff.
S3.quote: Five years for the thinking AI and three more for robots feels like a deadline more than a cliff.
fieldNote: With five years, Hana switches from defending her job to **planning a second skill**.
She downsizes the flat plan instead of dropping it, showing her **pragmatic middle** streak.
Union support is about **training and first refusal**, not blocking machines.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening testing and commissioning course, half paid by work
Buy a one-bed past the ring road instead of a two-bed
Ask the union to push for crews getting first go at robot jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a career's worth of warning, so nobody gets to act surprised. I'd probably say it to the apprentices too, because they're the ones who'll be around in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think ten years is enough for me. I'd be thirty-seven when the robots come. I could finish my jointing tickets, get the commissioning qualification, and be the person who looks after the machines rather than the person they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat I actually want, because a decade of steady wages pays down a lot. I'd do the commissioning course over two years, not one, so I'm not knackered. And around year five I'd ask to move to the team that tests new kit, before everyone else thinks of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit uneasy, because it's still the same end point. But I can plan for ten years, and planning makes me calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you were talking to one of the apprentices, what would you actually tell them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Callum, our apprentice, who's nineteen, to learn the jointing but not to stop there. Get the testing side, get the controls side, learn how the machines think. A nineteen-year-old who only knows how to splice cable will be thirty-two with nothing to sell when the robots turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd shelve the flat in the fast picture. What makes it okay here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time and the size of the loan. With ten years of wages I'd have paid off maybe a fifth of it before anything changes, and I'd have a second skill by then. It's not that I'm braver here, it's that the maths works.

say: Ten years is a **career's worth of warning**, so nobody gets to act surprised.
I'd pass that message on to the **apprentices**, who'll still be working in 2039.
think: At **thirty-seven** when robots arrive, I'd have time to finish every ticket and add commissioning.
I'd aim to **look after the machines** rather than be replaced by them.
do: Buy the **flat she actually wants** while wages are steady.
Spread the **commissioning course** over two years to avoid burning out.
Ask around **year five** to move to the team testing new equipment.
feel: Mostly fine, a little **uneasy**; **planning** is what makes her calm.
S4.quote: A nineteen-year-old who only knows how to splice cable will be thirty-two with nothing to sell when the robots turn up.
fieldNote: With a decade, Hana goes back to her **original life plan** and adds a second skill on top.
She explains the flat decision as **maths, not bravery**, which fits her pragmatic outlook.
Her advice to the **apprentice** shows she sees younger workers as more exposed than herself.

steps.text: Buy a two-bed flat near the river within three years
Take the commissioning course part time over two years
Ask in year five to join the new-equipment testing team

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The one by 2028, no question. It's not that robots come, it's that they come before I've got a second skill and before I own anything. What would help is the company paying for commissioning and testing courses for the crews now, not after, and a clear promise that we get first go at the machine jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who checks the machines. Everyone talks about who loses the job, but on a live cable a mistake kills somebody. Whatever does the joint, somebody who understands cable has to sign it off, and I'd like that somebody to still be a person for a long while.

headlineQuote: Whatever does the joint, somebody who understands cable has to sign it off, and I'd like that somebody to still be a person for a long while.
portrait: Hana is a **27-year-old cable jointer** on a city underground crew, renting alone and saving for a flat.
She takes pride in **tidy, solo craft** work and worries more about rent than AI in the calm pictures.
In the AGI pictures she plans to **become the machine minder**, through commissioning courses and robot pilot crews.
How fast it comes decides whether she **shelves, shrinks or keeps** her flat plan.
She keeps coming back to **safety**: someone who understands cable must check the work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would arrive before she has a second skill or owns a home.
whatWouldHelp: **Company-paid courses** in commissioning and testing for crews, starting now.
A promise that crews get **first go** at jobs running the new machines.
